clue.text: Move a pot marked "live dairy product"

indicators.note: to move things is to shift them around, so these letters are put into a new order

parts.note: fourteen letters taken as written, quotation mark ignored

explanation.surface: Someone is told to shift a jar labelled as containing live yoghurt.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks try to bind 'live dairy product' together as a label; in fact 'live' belongs with the fodder and only 'dairy product' defines.
explanation.definitionFit: Evaporated milk is tinned milk thickened by removing water, an example of something made in a dairy.

clue.text: Instrument, cembalo, Ivor's pounding, rampant

indicators.note: a rampant beast in heraldry rears up on its hind legs, and in a down clue rearing up means reading from the bottom

parts.note: the letters running across the end of the first word and the start of the second
surface padding: it only paints Ivor hammering at the keys

explanation.surface: Ivor is hammering away wildly at a harpsichord.
explanation.walkthrough: A cembalo is a harpsichord, which makes 'Instrument' look like a description of it; the answer is a different instrument hiding backwards inside the words, with 'pounding' only there for the picture.
explanation.definitionFit: The viola is a bowed string instrument, slightly larger than a violin, so it is one example of a musical instrument.

clue.text: Chat at length about Spar cashier's booth

indicators.note: to turn about is to face the other way, so the word is read in the opposite direction

parts.note: to yap is to talk on and on
to spar is to box in practice

explanation.surface: Someone gossips at length about the Spar convenience store.
explanation.walkthrough: Spar is a chain of convenience shops, so the capital letter disguises the verb meaning to box.
explanation.definitionFit: A pay-box is the small kiosk where a cashier takes money, as at a cinema or car park.

clue.text: Where BBC Question Time panel once sat for end-of-year update?

definitions.text: Where BBC Question Time panel once sat
definitions.meaning: first meaning, cryptic: the panel sat around the presenter Sir Robin Day
second meaning: a circular letter of family news sent with Christmas cards

explanation.surface: Where the Question Time panellists once gathered for an annual review.
explanation.walkthrough: Robin Day was the first chairman of the BBC political debate show Question Time, so his panel sat around him.
explanation.definitionFit: A round robin is a newsletter copied to many friends, typically sent at Christmas summarising the family's past year.

clue.text: I'll be seeing you regularly at last, dad

indicators.note: something done regularly happens at even intervals, so every other letter is kept

parts.note: the second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters

explanation.surface: A child finally says goodbye to their father, promising to see him often.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At last' looks like it should select a final letter, but the words are only fodder; the even letters across all three words give the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Ta-ta is a casual British farewell, used just as the phrase promising a future meeting is when parting.

clue.text: What might dispense tea into mug daily

indicators.note: going into something means ending up inside it

parts.note: mug and dial are both slang for face
a large urn serves tea at gatherings

explanation.surface: Something pours tea into a cup every day.
explanation.walkthrough: The mug wants to be a cup for the tea, but it is slang for a face, as is dial.
explanation.definitionFit: Diurnal means occurring every day or in daytime, a formal synonym of daily.

clue.text: Dull islands visited by granny and companion

indicators.note: a visitor comes inside the place visited

parts.note: I is the abbreviation for island, twice for the plural
nan is a familiar word for a grandmother
a mate is a friend

explanation.surface: A boring island holiday spent visiting grandma with a friend.
explanation.walkthrough: The plural 'islands' supplies two single-letter abbreviations, one either side of the grandmother.
explanation.definitionFit: Something inanimate is lifeless and lacking spirit, which is one figurative sense of being dull.

clue.text: Hole up in part of castle cracking

parts.note: the keep is a castle's central tower
cracking and out of sight are both slang for excellent

explanation.surface: A hole appears in a cracking castle wall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cracking' reads as splitting stone but is British slang for wonderful, matched by the old slang phrase meaning brilliant.
explanation.definitionFit: To hole up is to hide away somewhere, which is the same as staying where nobody can see you.

clue.text: Book delay is badly hampering western actor

parts.note: Daniel is a book of the Old Testament

indicators.note: to hamper is to hem in, so one piece is enclosed by another
something done badly is done wrong, so these letters are jumbled

parts.note: fodder taken as written
W is the abbreviation for western

explanation.surface: A book's publication is held up because an actor is caught in a western film.
explanation.walkthrough: The jumbled letters are split around the abbreviation for western; the result is the triple Oscar-winning British actor.
explanation.definitionFit: Daniel Day-Lewis is a famous British-Irish film star, so he is an example of a person who acts.

clue.text: One who tries to relieve pain in organ?

definitions.text: One who tries to relieve pain in organ?

parts.words: One who tries to relieve pain in organ?
parts.note: surface reading: a doctor easing a pain in a bodily organ such as the liver
setter's reading: an organ is also a newspaper or magazine, where a columnist answers readers' troubles

explanation.walkthrough: Organ here means a publication, and the pain is the distress readers write in about to the advice column.
explanation.definitionFit: An agony aunt writes a newspaper advice column replying to readers' personal problems, trying to ease their suffering.

clue.text: Handling string of sausages

indicators.note: a string is a run of consecutive items, so a run of consecutive letters is taken from inside

parts.note: the run inside, dropping the first two and last letters

explanation.surface: Someone is handling a long chain of linked sausages.
explanation.walkthrough: A string of sausages is a familiar butcher's phrase, which hides that 'string of' means a run of letters within the word.
explanation.definitionFit: Usage is the way something is treated or used, so it means the same as handling in the sense of treatment.

clue.text: Any minute now, ring daughter sulking

parts.note: 'in a mo' is British shorthand for in a moment
a ring is round like the letter O
D is the abbreviation for daughter

explanation.surface: Someone promises to phone their sulky daughter any minute.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ring' looks like a phone call but is just the round letter; 'mo' is a British colloquial moment.
explanation.definitionFit: To be in a mood is the British idiom for being sulky or bad-tempered.

clue.text: Popular, like duck — it's not teal!

definitions.note: a colour defined by what it is not

parts.note: what is in is fashionable
to dig something is slang for liking it
a duck is a score of nothing in cricket, so zero

explanation.surface: A duck is popular, and the speaker insists it is not a teal.
explanation.walkthrough: Teal is both a duck and a colour, so after 'duck' it reads as a bird; it is the colour, and the answer is a different shade.
explanation.definitionFit: Indigo is a deep blue-violet colour, a neighbour of the greenish-blue shade but distinct from it.

clue.text: Meeting in building

definitions.meaning: second meaning: putting something together from parts

explanation.surface: A meeting takes place inside a building.
explanation.walkthrough: Both words are present participles here, not nouns for a gathering and a structure.
explanation.definitionFit: People assembling are coming together, and assembling furniture is constructing it from parts.

clue.text: City stifled by left back for Bournemouth, a dirty sort

indicators.note: to be stifled is to be smothered, so this piece is wrapped inside

parts.note: L is the abbreviation for left
EC is the postcode area of the City of London

indicators.note: the back of a word is its final letter

parts.note: its last letter

explanation.surface: A football report: a city side is held back by Bournemouth's left back, a dirty player.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left back' looks like a football position, but 'back' belongs to Bournemouth. The City is London's financial district.
explanation.definitionFit: A lech is a lecherous man, one given to lewd behaviour, which is what a dirty sort suggests.

clue.text: Vulgar characters inside harem used up our time

parts.note: common means coarse or low-class

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means reading from bottom to top
the characters inside a word are those between its first and last letters

parts.note: the three letters between first and last

explanation.surface: Coarse people in a harem have wasted our time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Used up' reads as wasted, but in a down clue it is the instruction to read upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: The Common Era is the neutral name for the dating system of the present age, so it is the period we live in.

clue.text: Doctor is against fruit if an adult succumbs to temperature

indicators.note: to succumb to something is to give way to it, so one letter yields its place to another

parts.note: con is the argument against, as in pros and cons
a sultana is a dried grape
A is the abbreviation for adult, as in film certificates
T is the abbreviation for temperature

explanation.surface: A doctor objects to fruit because an adult went down with a fever.
explanation.walkthrough: The final adult letter of the dried fruit is swapped for the temperature letter.
explanation.definitionFit: In Britain a consultant is a senior hospital doctor in charge of a specialty.

clue.text: A jolly time binding one's Frost poems finally in peaceful periods

indicators.note: to bind is to tie round, so one piece is wrapped around another

parts.note: taken as written
a jolly is old slang for a Royal Marine, RM
I for one plus the S
T is the abbreviation for time
frost is frozen water

indicators.note: finally points to the very end of a word

parts.note: its last letter

explanation.surface: A happy occasion collecting Robert Frost's poems on peace.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Frost' looks like the American poet beside 'poems', but it is plain frozen water. A jolly is crossword slang for a Royal Marine.
explanation.definitionFit: Armistices are truces agreed between warring sides, stretches of time when fighting stops.

clue.text: Reportedly glimpse swallow — it may be in rocky pool

definitions.text: it may be in rocky pool

indicators.note: what is reported is passed on by word of mouth, so the sound matters rather than the spelling

parts.note: to see is to glimpse, and a slug is a gulp of drink

explanation.surface: Someone claims to have spotted a swallow, the bird, near a rock pool.
explanation.walkthrough: The swallow is not the bird but a mouthful of drink, a slug.
explanation.definitionFit: A sea slug is a soft marine mollusc often found by beachcombers among the seaweed of tidal rock pools.

clue.text: I put back tissue husband's left

indicators.note: putting something back turns it round to face the other way
something that has left has gone away, so it is removed

parts.note: flesh is soft body tissue
H is the abbreviation for husband

explanation.surface: Someone replaces the tissue box after the husband has gone.
explanation.walkthrough: The body tissue is turned round, and then its new first letter, the husband, departs.
explanation.definitionFit: 'I' names the speaker's own identity, and one's self is the ego or person a person is.

clue.text: Decent son replacing old Ford's light at the front

indicators.note: to replace is to take another's place, so one letter is swapped for another

parts.note: the Model T was Ford's early mass-produced car
S is the abbreviation for son

indicators.note: the front of a word is its opening letter

parts.note: its first letter

explanation.surface: A decent son swaps the headlight on his vintage Ford.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ford's light at the front' sounds like a headlamp; it is the first letter of 'light' inside the old car, swapped out for the son.
explanation.definitionFit: Modest can mean decorous and proper in dress or behaviour, a sense shared with decent.

clue.text: Sponge from far side of beach area Charlie turned over

indicators.note: turning something over puts it the other way round
the far side of a word is its last letter

parts.note: its last letter
A is the abbreviation for area
a charlie is British slang for a silly person

explanation.surface: A sponge washed up on the far side of a beach where Charlie fell over.
explanation.walkthrough: Charlie looks like a person or the C of the radio alphabet, but here it is British slang for an idiot.
explanation.definitionFit: A loofah is the dried fibrous pod of a gourd used as a bath sponge for scrubbing skin.

clue.text: Air passes through these branches on birch when windy

indicators.note: windy weather blows things about, so these letters are tossed into a new order

parts.note: fodder taken as written

explanation.surface: On a windy day the wind blows through the branches of a birch tree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Branches' looks like part of the tree scene but belongs with the definition: the airways of the lungs branch like a tree.
explanation.definitionFit: The bronchi are the two main airways that fork from the windpipe into the lungs, carrying breath inward.

clue.text: One getting weepy, Old Yeller, in town?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a person who sheds tears
second meaning: the official who once shouted announcements in a town's streets

explanation.walkthrough: Old Yeller is a tearjerker film about a dog, which makes the whole clue look like a weepy movie; read literally it is an old-time shouter of public news.
explanation.definitionFit: A crier is anyone who weeps, and a town crier was the official who proclaimed public news by calling out loudly.

clue.text: Outstanding doughnut chewed, half gone

parts.note: a ring doughnut has the shape of the letter O

indicators.note: if half of something has gone, only the other half is left

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An excellent doughnut, half of it already eaten.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outstanding' suggests excellent, but here it means unpaid; the first half of the six-letter word drops away.
explanation.definitionFit: An outstanding debt is one still to be paid, which is money owed.

clue.text: Turn from Little and Large entertaining hotel

indicators.note: to entertain a guest is to have them in your home, so one piece holds another

parts.note: wee is Scottish for small
L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large
H is hotel in the radio alphabet

explanation.surface: A comedy act from the double act Little and Large performing at a hotel.
explanation.walkthrough: Little and Large were a British TV comedy double act, which makes 'Turn' look like a stage act.
explanation.definitionFit: To wheel is to turn round in a circle, as soldiers or birds do when changing direction.

clue.text: Scrap request for Spooner's cod?

indicators.note: Reverend Spooner famously swapped the opening sounds of words

parts.note: a scrap is a fight and a request is a wish; swap their opening sounds

explanation.surface: Someone asks for scraps for cod, as if ordering at a chip shop.
explanation.walkthrough: Scraps are the bits of loose batter a British chip shop gives away, which makes the fish-shop picture convincing.
explanation.definitionFit: Cod is the classic example of white fish, the category of pale-fleshed sea fish.

clue.text: Rapper worries politician? That's a joke

parts.note: Shaggy is a Jamaican-American reggae and dancehall singer
worry dogs a person, following them persistently
a Tory is a member of the UK Conservative Party

explanation.surface: A rapper fretting about a politician is laughed off as ridiculous.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Worries' reads as a noun, a rapper's anxieties, but it is the verb meaning hounds.
explanation.definitionFit: A shaggy-dog story is a long rambling anecdote whose humour lies in its pointless anticlimax, a type of joke.
